analysis.one_liner: Caps payday loan interest and fees, bans rollovers, and bars criminal debt-collection threats.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would cap payday loan interest at 36% and ban repeated rollovers, never received a committee vote and died in the House Financial Services Committee with 31 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made payday lending illegal in any state that does not license and strictly regulate it under federal minimum standards. It capped the annual interest rate at 36% (or lower where state law is stricter), limited loan principal to $300, capped administrative fees at $5, banned rolling over or immediately re-taking loans, and barred lenders from threatening borrowers with criminal charges over bounced checks. It also banned forced arbitration clauses, required public hearings before lenders could be licensed, and stopped banks from making payday loans above the rate cap or financing noncompliant lenders.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income borrowers who use payday loans. The bill targets the core mechanics of the industry: interest and fee caps [S3], a ban on rollovers and new loans within 30 days [S3], a ban on criminal or civil proceedings or threats tied to bounced-check repayment [S3], mandatory disclosures of borrower rights [S3], a private right of action with $1,000 statutory damages per violation plus attorney's fees [S3], and licensing requirements including $50,000 surety bonds per location payable to consumers for violations [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual interest rate on any payday loan at the lesser of 36% or the state's maximum for comparable small loans, and caps the administrative fee at $5.
Bans rolling over loans or issuing a new loan within 30 days of a prior one, the practice that traps borrowers in repeat cycles of debt.
Prohibits lenders from initiating or threatening criminal action or civil proceedings over a borrower's failure to repay, including over checks drawn on accounts with insufficient funds.

Bans forced arbitration clauses in payday loan contracts and gives borrowers a private right to sue for actual, consequential, and punitive damages, $1,000 statutory damages per violation, and attorney's fees.

Requires every state to license and vet payday lenders, with public hearings, surety bonds of at least $50,000 per location payable to consumers, civil penalties of at least $1,000 per violation, and criminal penalties for unlicensed lending.
Bars banks from making payday loans above 36% interest or lending to payday lenders that do not comply with federal and state law, closing the 'rent-a-bank' channel around state rate caps.

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders, whose business model of high fees and repeated rollovers would become unlawful, and banks that partner with or finance payday lenders. Borrowers in states that decline to adopt the required licensing law would lose access to legal short-term credit entirely, since payday lending would be prohibited there.

drawbacks.text: The strictest defenders of payday borrowers acknowledge the cap is binding: at 36% annual interest plus a $5 fee, a two-week $300 loan yields roughly $3.60 in interest, which may not cover the lender's cost of a small, default-prone loan. The bill could eliminate legal payday lending in states that choose not to pass a compliant licensing law, and some borrowers who lack access to banks or credit cards could be pushed toward illegal or unregulated lenders.

The bill sets federal minimum standards but lets each state decide whether to license payday lending at all, so its protections would not apply uniformly; in non-adopting states the entire industry would simply be shut down rather than reformed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are strong and directly aimed at the practices that make payday loans costly — rollover debt, criminal-collection threats, hidden fees, and arbitration clauses that block lawsuits. The main honest tradeoff is availability: the 36% cap plus fee limits may make small short-term loans unprofitable, and states that decline to license the industry would see it disappear rather than become affordable. For borrowers who today pay triple-digit annual rates, the trade favors protection; for borrowers with no other credit option, the bill offers no replacement product.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, sent to its financial institutions subcommittee in April 2001, and no further action was taken before the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush introduced the Payday Borrower Protection Act of 2001 on March 29, 2001, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
On April 24, 2001, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress.

The bill attracted 31 cosponsors — 28 of 208 House Democrats and 3 of 223 House Republicans — but the committee never held a markup or brought it to a vote before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday lenders, who faced no federal rate cap, rollover limits, or licensing requirements, continued operating under the pre-existing patchwork of state rules. Borrowers gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Rep. Bobby Rush
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 29, 2001 and delivered introductory remarks.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, sent it to the Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit Subcommittee, and never held a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided: 28 Democrats and 3 Republicans cosponsored, and no roll-call vote was ever taken, so the partisan split on the merits is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would cap their annual interest rate at 36%, cap fees, and ban rollovers, directly eliminating the fee-and-reloan cycle that produces most industry revenue. Lenders' interest in the bill ran against borrowers, who would keep more of their paychecks if it passed.

The bill bars banks from making payday loans above 36% interest or financing payday lenders that do not fully comply with state law, cutting off the bank-partnership channel used to avoid state rate caps. That channel raised loan costs for borrowers.
The bill bans charging any additional fee or premium for credit insurance sold alongside a payday loan, ending an add-on charge to borrowers.

The bill bans forced arbitration clauses in payday loan contracts, keeping borrower disputes in court where class actions and statutory damages are available. Consumers benefit from access to court remedies.
